scenes.narration: When people talk about career decisions, they often imagine there is one right answer hiding somewhere.

vars.title: Better Decisions Come from Better Criteria

scenes.narration: The right job. The right major. The right city, or the right path.

vars.label: The myth
vars.heading: One Right Answer
vars.chips: The right job,The right major,The right city,The right path

scenes.narration: But most strong career decisions do not come from finding a perfect answer. They come from choosing among several good options with clear criteria and good judgment.

vars.statement: Strong Decisions Come from Good Options
vars.lines: Choose among several good options|Bring clear criteria and good judgment

scenes.narration: One reason career decisions feel hard is that people often decide under pressure.
They compare themselves to others. They focus on one factor like salary or prestige.

vars.label: Under pressure
vars.heading: What Pressure Looks Like
vars.point2: Fixing on one factor like salary

scenes.narration: Or they stay committed to a path because they have already invested time into it, even if it is no longer the best fit.

vars.statement: Staying on a Path You Already Paid For
vars.lines: Time already invested|Even when the fit is weak

scenes.narration: The sunk cost problem is especially common. It happens when someone thinks, "I already put so much time into this, I cannot change now," even when the future fit is weak.

pointCues: I already put so much time

vars.notes: The time is spent either way

scenes.narration: Better decisions become possible when you shift from pressure to process. Here is a simple process.
First, define what success means for you over the next three to five years. Not forever. Just the next stage.

chipCues: the next three to five years

vars.heading: Define What Success Means to You
vars.chips: The next three to five years,Not forever,Just the next stage

scenes.narration: Do you care most about learning? Security? Income? Flexibility? Meaning? Mentorship? Or growth?
Second, broaden your options. If you only compare one job to one other job, your frame is too narrow.

vars.heading: Broaden Your Options
vars.chips: One job,One other job,Too narrow a frame

scenes.narration: Instead, list three to five possible paths. They might be different roles, different industries, different learning opportunities, or different next steps.
Third, compare those options using your criteria. That is where a tool like a career map becomes helpful.

vars.lines: Judge each path by what matters to you|A career map makes the comparison visible

scenes.narration: You are not just asking, "Which one sounds good?" You are asking, "Which one fits what matters to me?"

vars.bTitle: Which one fits what matters to me?

scenes.narration: Fourth, notice what you still do not know. Some decisions cannot be solved only by thinking. Sometimes you need more evidence.

chipCues: what you still do not know
cannot be solved only by thinking

vars.heading: Notice What You Do Not Know
vars.chips: Gaps in what you know,Not solved by thinking,More evidence

scenes.narration: That might mean talking to someone in the field, doing a short project, shadowing, reading job postings, or testing a new skill.

chipCues: talking to someone in the field

vars.label: Gather evidence
vars.heading: Ways to Learn More
vars.chips: Talk to someone,Do a short project,Shadow,Read job postings,Test a new skill

scenes.narration: AI can be useful here too. It can help you brainstorm additional options, summarize what different roles involve, or show you where your comparison may be incomplete.

vars.label: Using AI
vars.heading: Where AI Helps
vars.point3: Show where your comparison is thin

scenes.narration: But it should not make the decision for you. The point of this module is not to make every decision easy.

vars.statement: You Make the Decision, Not the Tool

scenes.narration: The point is to help you build a repeatable process so that career decisions become more thoughtful, less reactive, and more grounded in what you actually value.

stepCues: grounded in what you actually value

vars.label: The takeaway
vars.heading: A Repeatable Process
vars.subBeats: Same four steps, every time|Use it on any career decision

scenes.narration: Once you know how to make one good decision, you can use that skill again and again.

vars.next: Use the same four steps on your next decision
